title: Creation and evolution
hookLine: many Christians accept evolution as God's way of creating; others read Genesis more literally

cards: A shell pressed into stone, on a museum shelf with a card beside it. A family stops to look. One child reads the card aloud.
Another asks, but didn't God make the world in six days? The parents glance at each other, because they read Genesis differently, and they both go to the same church.
It isn't a fight between church and science, at least not in that family. It's a question about how to read a very old page. Today: creation and evolution.

teach.b: Genesis opens with days: light on the first, sky on the second, land and plants on the third, and on to the seventh, when God rests. Christians who disagree here can both call that chapter true.

They differ on what kind of true. Some read the days as ordinary days and the earth as young, and see evolution as a story that doesn't fit the page; taking the text at its plainest, they say, is how they honor it.

teach.h: READ PLAIN, OR READ AS A PATTERN?
teach.b: Others accept evolution as the way God made living things, over a very long time, and read the days as a pattern, a week of work and rest, telling who made the world and why, not a timetable of how.
Readers of plain days point to the commandment in Exodus: "For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is."

teach.h: A THOUSAND YEARS AS ONE DAY.
teach.b: Readers of a pattern point to a psalm, "For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past," and to the second letter of Peter: "one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day."

And an old voice: Augustine, bishop of Hippo, wrote a book on the literal meaning of Genesis, warning Christians not to talk nonsense about the natural world in front of people who know it well, because it makes scripture look foolish.
He wrote for his own day, not ours, but took the page and the world seriously.
Under the arguing, both share yesterday's teaching: in six days or across ages, the world is a gift, made on purpose, by the God of every one of those days.

how: Christians differ on Genesis and evolution: some churches and schools teach a young earth and six ordinary days, while others accept evolution and teach Genesis as God's account of who made the world and why.

games.why: Christians on both sides of the question say God made the world. they differ on how to read the days, not on who the maker is.

practice: Find a stone, or a photo of one, and look closely at its color, cracks and layers. However you read Genesis, it was here before you and will likely outlast you.
If you pray, say slowly, a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday; if not, stay with the stone and the time it holds.

wordCard.voice: Creation and evolution. Some Christians read Genesis as plain days, some as a pattern with room for evolution. Both say God made the world.

orig.note: Hebrew: day. The word for each of the days in Genesis 1, read by some as ordinary days, by others as a pattern.

carryVoice: Your line: god of all time. Six days or long ages, one maker. That's today, done.
